subsection: 4. Parnell’s fall, Redmond’s leadership and Home Rule’s rivals, 1886–1914

notes.h: The Plan of Campaign, Pigott and the Special Commission (1886–1890)
notes.b: By 1886 Parnell had built a disciplined Irish Party and an alliance with Gladstone's Liberals, and the First Home Rule Bill had just been defeated in the Commons in June 1886. Over the next four years he kept his distance from agrarian violence, and his enemies tried to destroy him with forged evidence and failed.
points: Background: Parnell had been chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party since 1880, and in the 1885 election the party won 85 of the 103 Irish seats. This strength is why Liberals and Conservatives alike had to take Home Rule seriously.

The Plan of Campaign (October 1886) was launched by William O’Brien, John Dillon and Timothy Harrington. Tenants offered what they thought a fair rent and, if the landlord refused it, paid it into a fund instead.

Parnell did not endorse the Plan, because he feared that evictions and violence would alarm British Liberals. His main concern was the Liberal alliance, so he spent much of 1887–89 away from Ireland and the daily running of the party.

In March 1887 The Times began a series called Parnellism and Crime. On 18 April 1887 it printed a letter, apparently signed by Parnell, that excused the Phoenix Park murders (the killing of Lord Frederick Cavendish and T.H. Burke in May 1882), so it aimed to link him to assassination.
The letter was one of several forged by Richard Pigott, a discredited Dublin journalist, who sold them to The Times.
The government set up a Special Commission of three judges in 1888, by Act of Parliament, to examine the charges against Parnell and about 65 other Irish MPs. It sat from 1888 into 1889.

Under cross-examination by Sir Charles Russell, Parnell’s counsel (lawyer), in February 1889 Pigott collapsed. He had misspelled the word hesitancy in the same way as in the forged letter, which exposed the forgery, and he fled to Madrid, where he shot himself on 1 March 1889.
Parnell was cheered by MPs in the Commons and visited Gladstone at Hawarden in December 1889. In 1890 The Times paid him £5,000 in an out-of-court settlement.

The Commission’s report (February 1890) rejected the forged letters, though it criticised the methods of the Land League (the tenant organisation of the Land War). Parnell now stood at the height of his reputation.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the Pigott forgeries failed: the answer is the misspelling of hesitancy and Pigott’s collapse under cross-examination. Remember that The Times paid a settlement; Parnell did not win damages in court.

notes.h: The O’Shea divorce and the split (1890–1891)
notes.b: Parnell’s private life, hidden for years, now decided his career. The divorce case of November 1890 turned the Liberal alliance and the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) against him and split the party.
points: Parnell had lived with Katharine O’Shea for years. Her husband Captain William O’Shea, a former Irish Party MP, filed for divorce in December 1889 and named Parnell as co-respondent (the man accused of adultery with the wife).
The case was heard on 15–17 November 1890. Parnell did not contest it, so a decree nisi (the first order ending the marriage) was granted.

On 25 November the Irish Party re-elected Parnell as chairman, before Gladstone’s letter to John Morley was published. The letter made Gladstone’s position plain: his leadership of the Liberals would be made almost useless if Parnell stayed.
Non-conformist Liberals threatened to desert Gladstone, and the pressure on him to break with Parnell grew.
notes.tip: Explain why the Liberals turned against him: Gladstone’s letter to Morley and the threat of non-conformist Liberals to desert him.

notes.h: Committee Room 15, the two parties and Parnell’s death (1890–1891)
notes.b: Parnell refused to step aside, so the pressure from the Liberals turned into an open fight inside his own party and in the country.
points: On 29 November Parnell issued a manifesto, To the People of Ireland. It attacked the Liberals and disclosed details of private talks with Gladstone, and it deepened the bitterness.

On 3 December 1890 the Catholic bishops, with Archbishop Walsh prominent, condemned Parnell as unfit to lead. The manifesto came first, on 29 November; the bishops’ condemnation followed on 3 December.
The debate in Committee Room 15 at Westminster lasted from 1 to 6 December 1890. On 6 December about 45 MPs led by Justin McCarthy walked out, leaving a minority of about 26–28 with Parnell.

The anti-Parnellites (the majority) included Dillon, William O’Brien, McCarthy and the fierce critic Tim Healy, and were later organised as the Irish National Federation (1891). The Parnellites kept control of the Irish National League.

Parnell’s candidates lost by-elections in North Kilkenny (December 1890), North Sligo (April 1891) and Carlow (July 1891), in vicious campaigns, which showed that the country as well as the party had turned against him.
He married Katharine on 25 June 1891 and died at Brighton on 6 October 1891, aged 45. He was buried at Glasnevin, and a very large crowd attended.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions on why Parnell fell expect the divorce, Gladstone’s letter, the bishops and the split, with dates. Explain why the Liberals and the Church each turned against him, not just that they did. Keep the Irish National League (Parnellites) apart from the Irish National Federation (anti-Parnellites).

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Stewart Parnell (part 2: 1886–1891 and overall evaluation)
notes.b: This part covers the years of Parnell’s peak influence, his fall and the overall judgement. The strengths and weaknesses below are the usual basis for essays on him.
points: What he did: between 1886 and 1890 he combined an alliance with Gladstone with firm control over a disciplined party of about 85 MPs. He was born in 1846 and was 45 when he died, so his career ended while he was still in his prime.
He was a participant in the Pigott and O’Shea affairs. He lost control of events after the divorce, when his refusal to step aside split the movement.
Contemporary nationalists were divided: the Parnellites saw him as a leader betrayed by Liberals and bishops, while the anti-Parnellites saw a leader who put himself above the cause.
Contemporary unionists (opponents of Home Rule) saw him as a dangerous agitator, until the Pigott collapse made The Times and his accusers look foolish.
Strengths: party discipline, tactical skill, ability to unite Fenians (physical-force nationalists), land reformers and constitutionalists, and a clear command of Commons procedure.

Weaknesses: aloofness and an autocratic style, dependence on the Liberals, ambiguity about violence in the Land War, and a private life that he did not manage, which handed his enemies the means to destroy him.

Historians differ: F.S.L. Lyons in Charles Stewart Parnell (1977) stresses the tragic collision of ambition and scandal. Paul Bew in C.S. Parnell (1980) presents a conservative landlord politician whose strategy had limits.
His legacy was the idea of an independent Irish party. He also left the Parnell legend of a betrayed leader, a martyr, which later nationalists and writers, including Yeats and Joyce, drew on.
notes.tip: In a Parnell essay, state your judgement at the start, then pair points with evidence: discipline and the Liberal alliance against aloofness, dependence on the Liberals and the divorce. Treat the Pigott triumph as the high point and the split as the fall, and name Lyons or Bew.

notes.h: The Second Home Rule Bill and the divided party (1891–1900)
notes.b: Gladstone’s last attempt at Home Rule was killed by the House of Lords, which could reject a bill passed by the Commons. The Irish Party then spent the 1890s in feud.
points: The Liberals returned to office after the 1892 election with a small majority that depended on the Irish MPs. Gladstone, aged 83, introduced the Second Home Rule Bill on 13 February 1893.

The Bill proposed an Irish legislature of two houses, and it kept a reduced number of Irish MPs at Westminster, to meet the objection that Ireland would otherwise be excluded from the parliament that still ruled the empire.
The Commons passed the Bill in September 1893 by 301 votes to 267, after eighty-two sittings, so the elected house backed it and only the Lords stood in the way.
The House of Lords threw it out on 8 September 1893 by 419 votes to 41, so a huge Conservative and Unionist majority in the Lords outweighed the Commons. Gladstone retired in March 1894.
Unionists had mobilised against the Bill, so Ulster resistance was already organised, notably at the Ulster Convention in Belfast in June 1892.

The Conservatives under Salisbury won the 1895 election, and Unionist governments held office for most of the next ten years. They tried to kill Home Rule with kindness, through land purchase, local government and the Congested Districts Board.
In the 1890s the Irish National Federation (Dillon and McCarthy), Healy’s followers and Redmond’s small Parnellite group fought each other, and voters became disillusioned.

The United Irish League was founded by William O’Brien at Westport, Co. Mayo, in January 1898 to revive the land agitation in the west. Do not confuse it with the Irish National League or the Irish National Federation.
The parties reunited in January 1900, and Redmond was elected chairman in February 1900.
notes.tip: For why the 1893 Bill failed, the answer is the Lords. For why the party was divided in the 1890s, give the Parnell split, the three rival groups and the voters’ disillusion.

notes.b: Redmond rebuilt the party, won land reform and then used the Liberals’ dependence on his votes to put Home Rule on the statute book. The last step came at a price in Ulster.
points: Redmond and William O’Brien took part in the Land Conference of December 1902–January 1903, with landlord representatives, which led to the Wyndham Act (1903).

In May 1907 a national convention of the party rejected the Irish Council Bill, a limited devolution scheme introduced by Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell. It offered less than Home Rule, so the party refused it.
Two general elections in 1910 (January and December) left the Liberals short of a majority without Irish nationalist votes. The nationalist MPs numbered in the low 80s and held the balance.

The Lords rejected the People’s Budget (1909), so the Liberals, backed by Redmond’s party, passed the Parliament Act (1911). It removed the Lords’ veto, leaving only a delay of two years; it did not itself grant Home Rule.
Asquith introduced the Third Home Rule Bill in April 1912. It became law on 18 September 1914, and a Suspensory Act held it back until the end of the war, which Redmond accepted.

Under pressure from the unionist threat, in March 1914 Asquith proposed that Ulster counties could opt out for six years. Redmond, who had resisted, accepted it, a concession he had previously refused.
In June 1914 Redmond insisted that 25 of his nominees join the Irish Volunteers’ provisional committee, and the committee accepted, so he gained control of the new force.
notes.tip: Remember that the Parliament Act removed the veto but did not grant Home Rule; keep the Irish Council Bill (1907, rejected) apart from the Home Rule Bills. For ‘how far did Home Rule succeed’, set the Act of 1914 against the Lords’ veto in 1893 and the unsolved Ulster question.

notes.b: Redmond led the reunited party for eighteen years and believed that Home Rule could be won by constitutional methods and kept by loyalty to the empire. The First World War wrecked that belief.
points: John Redmond (1856–1918) was born at Ballytrent, Co. Wexford, into a Catholic landed family. He was educated at Clongowes, became a barrister and was an MP from 1881.
He stayed loyal to Parnell in 1890, which is why he led the small Parnellite group after Parnell died in 1891. He sat for Waterford City from 1891 until his death in March 1918.
As a participant he reunited the party in 1900 and negotiated the Land Conference, the 1911 Parliament Act and the 1912 Bill, relying on his control of the party’s votes.
Contemporary nationalists generally admired him as the leader who delivered Home Rule. Critics such as Griffith and the IRB attacked his reliance on Liberal goodwill.
In August 1914 he offered the Volunteers for the defence of Ireland. His Woodenbridge speech, in Co. Wicklow on 20 September 1914, urged them to fight in the war, and this split the Irish Volunteers.
The great majority followed him as the National Volunteers, and about 10,000–12,000 stayed with Eoin MacNeill’s Irish Volunteers (estimates vary).
Strengths: party management, which kept the reunited party together, parliamentary skill, a genuine achievement in land and the Home Rule Act, and personal integrity.
Weaknesses: dependence on the Liberals, failure to resolve the Ulster problem, acceptance of partition in principle in 1914 and poor judgement of the new separatism.

Historians differ: Denis Gwynn’s The Life of John Redmond (1932) is sympathetic, and Dermot Meleady’s John Redmond: The National Leader (2013) presents a statesman wrecked by war. Others see a leader out of touch with the new generation.
notes.tip: For a profile of Redmond, give dates: birth and career, loyalty to Parnell, reunion in 1900, the Land Conference, the Parliament Act, the Home Rule Act, Woodenbridge and the split. A bare list without dates scores less. For Redmond against Carson, state who was more effective and name each one’s limits: Redmond on Ulster and the war.

notes.b: Separatism means full independence from Britain, whereas Home Rule meant a parliament in Dublin within the United Kingdom. Arthur Griffith proposed a separatist policy of abstention and economic self-reliance as an alternative to Home Rule.
points: Arthur Griffith, a Dublin printer and journalist, founded the newspaper The United Irishman in 1899 with William Rooney.
Cumann na nGaedheal was founded in 1900 to unite groups promoting Irish language, industry and the national cause, so it gathered scattered separatist and cultural groups in one body.

In The Resurrection of Hungary (1904) Griffith argued that Ireland should follow Hungary, which had won its own parliament within a dual monarchy (Austria-Hungary, in 1867) after refusing to sit in the Vienna parliament. This is abstentionism: refusing to attend the imperial parliament.

At a convention in November 1905 the National Council adopted what became the Sinn Féin policy: abstain from Westminster, set up a national assembly in Dublin and protect Irish industry with tariffs (taxes on imports).
The weekly Sinn Féin followed in 1906. The Dungannon Clubs of Bulmer Hobson merged with Cumann na nGaedheal in 1907 as the Sinn Féin League, and the party was fully constituted as Sinn Féin in 1908.
In the North Leitrim by-election of February 1908 the Sinn Féin candidate C.J. Dolan, who had left the Irish Party, was beaten by roughly three to one.
Sinn Féin lost support after 1908 and the party remained small, but its ideas about abstention and self-reliance were revived in 1917.
notes.tip: Describe the Sinn Féin of Griffith’s dual-monarchy policy, not the republican party after 1917; that is the common error. Give the 1905 policy points (abstention, assembly, protection) and North Leitrim as the reason it stayed small.

notes.h: The IRB revival and the Irish Volunteers (1907–1914)
notes.b: The IRB (Irish Republican Brotherhood) was the secret Fenian organisation committed to physical force. A younger generation revived it, and the Ulster Volunteers (the unionist armed force formed in 1913) became the model for militarism, meaning armed volunteer forces used as a political instrument.
points: Tom Clarke, a Fenian who had served about fifteen years in prison, returned from the USA in December 1907 and opened a tobacconist’s shop in Dublin.
With Bulmer Hobson and Seán Mac Diarmada, Clarke revived the IRB and founded the paper Irish Freedom (1910).
Eoin MacNeill’s article The North Began, published in An Claidheamh Soluis on 1 November 1913, argued that the Ulster Volunteers had shown that Irishmen could arm and organise to defend their rights.
The Irish Volunteers were founded on 25 November 1913 at the Rotunda Rink in Dublin. MacNeill became chairman, and IRB men worked behind the scenes, so the separatists had a hidden influence.
Cumann na mBan, a women’s organisation to support the Volunteers, was founded in April 1914.
The Howth gun-running on 26 July 1914 landed about 900 rifles from Erskine Childers’s yacht Asgard. British soldiers then fired on a crowd at Bachelor’s Walk in Dublin, killing four.
After Redmond’s Woodenbridge speech the Volunteers split in September 1914: the majority became the National Volunteers and a minority kept the name Irish Volunteers.
notes.tip: For the Irish Volunteers give what prompted them (the Ulster Volunteers and MacNeill’s article), the date and place of founding, the chairman, IRB influence, Howth and the split over Redmond’s call to fight. Keep the Irish, Ulster and National Volunteers apart.

notes.h: Assessment: Parnell, Redmond and the alternatives to Home Rule
notes.b: The period shows constitutional nationalism at its strongest and the first serious challenge to it. Examiners reward a clear judgement backed by paired points.
points: Achievements of the Home Rule movement: a united parliamentary party, land reform and, by 1914, a Home Rule Act on the statute book.
Limits: Parnell’s fall wasted a decade, the Lords killed the 1893 Bill, and the Ulster question remained unsolved in 1914, so Home Rule was law but had not yet taken effect.
Sinn Féin and the IRB offered a separatist alternative, but before 1914 they were small and divided. Their growth after 1914 owed more to war and the 1916 Rising than to their own efforts.

Contemporary unionists judged Redmond a threat to the Union because Home Rule would weaken it; separatists judged him too moderate because he sought less than independence; most nationalists in 1914 supported him.
Historians now often argue that Home Rule was not doomed before 1914 and that its collapse came from the war, the Rising and the conscription crisis.
notes.tip: Students lose marks by describing events without saying how far the aim was reached. State a verdict, then give each point a year and a named person, and end each paragraph with a one-line verdict.

The use of armed volunteer forces as a political instrument, as the Ulster Volunteers and the Irish Volunteers did from 1913.

The majority of the Irish Party who rejected Parnell’s leadership in December 1890 and later formed the Irish National Federation.
The land and political organisation founded by William O’Brien in 1898, which became Redmond’s grassroots machine.
Griffith’s party, adopted in 1905, based on abstention from Westminster, a Dublin assembly, dual monarchy and economic self-sufficiency.
The nationalist force founded in November 1913 in response to the Ulster Volunteers, which split in September 1914.
The Austro-Hungarian model, in which Hungary had its own parliament under a shared monarch, proposed by Griffith for Ireland.
